 Trump has somehow made free money toxic to Americans
 The president hopes a promise of $5,000 checks, as well as other handouts, will swing the election. These voters think otherwise. 
 Play 
 Soboroff gives Trump’s $5K promise a reality check 
 September 13, 2026 / 04:24 
 By  
 Joseph Zeballos-Roig 
 Oct. 21, 2026, 6:00 AM EDT 
 Inflation has outpaced wage gains for six months and counting. Gas prices have averaged over $4 per gallon for most of the past six months. It’s unlikely consumer prices will come down anytime soon — Congress is on the sidelines, and the president shows no signs of reversing course on his tariffs and the never-ending Iran war.
 Under these bleak circumstances, you would think receiving cash with no strings attached from the federal government would be something people would welcome with open arms. But President Donald Trump has achieved something remarkable: He’s made free money toxic to many Americans.
 Since early September, Trump has promised to issue a $5,000 “dividend” to every American adult if Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. He has repeated this pledge throughout his midterm rally blitz. Despite its eye-watering $1 trillion price tag and the fact that federal law bars election-related payouts, Trump hopes the promise will butter up frustrated voters.
 “If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pockets,” the president said at a Georgia campaign rally on Friday. He implored the audience to trust him: “I’ll do it, I always do it.”
 Multiple polls demonstrate that most Americans aren’t buying Trump’s $5,000 dividend promises or don’t think it’s a good idea.
 The $5,000 checks are just the largest of several freebies Trump has offered. Less than 24 hours later, he also announced $500 “refund” checks to Americans who receive health insurance through the Affordable Care Act, saying they were overcharged for their premiums. The White House estimated the checks will reach about 1 million Americans in 30 states.
 Then, in early October, the Trump administration launched another one-time payment program: $90 for about 20 million seniors receiving medical coverage through Medicare. This initiative is funded by the questionable use of a $2 billion fund for improving Medicare.
 I spoke to three people who have received Trump’s last-ditch payouts. Two of them received the Medicare payment, and the other received the Obamacare one. All described a feeling of disgust at what they called receiving a “bribe” for their votes.
 Play 
 Even Republicans are skeptical of Trump’s ability to deliver on his $5,000 promise 
 September 12, 2026 / 08:17 
 On Oct. 8, Cynthia Heim, a former IT worker who lives just outside of Wilmington, Delaware, spotted a strange email in her inbox. It was Trump taking credit for the Medicare payment, similar to what he did during the first pandemic stimulus checks of 2020. She immediately deleted the email and cast it into the digital ether.
 “Obviously, I was thinking this is trying to bribe people. It was just a weird timing of when he decided to send this out,” Heim told me. “I could think of more things that those $2 billion could have been used for.”
 Heim has felt inflation chomp into her finances like many Americans. Her pension and monthly Social Security check don’t buy as many things as they used to. She’s still paying off a mortgage, and dining out is no longer an affordable luxury to splurge on. Cheap ramen is now a staple she regularly eats alongside her adult son, who lives with her.
 “I have a 401k that I’ve already dipped into twice this year,” she said. “This past year is the worst that I have felt.”
 Whether the president knows it or not, Trump is copying the playbook of populist governments with awful economic track records.
 But despite the pressure, Heim didn’t want to use what she felt was tainted money. Instead, she donated all of it to the Democratic National Committee.
 Alison Butler, a former economics professor residing in Washington, D.C., had a similar reaction when she noticed a $90 deposit in her bank account earlier this month.
 “It doesn’t feel like money I am entitled to,” she told me. “And if I’m not entitled to it, I don’t want to keep it.”
 Butler, another registered Democrat, split the money into two donations. One went to an initiative that delivers books to Washington prisons, and the other went to a mental health nonprofit that connects formerly incarcerated people with therapists.
 Play 
 ‘Democracy is not for sale’: Dem BLASTS Trump bragging about his power and proposed $5K checks 
 October 18, 2026 / 09:47 
 Their reactions to the payouts are not terribly surprising, given the poor reception for the original “dividend” pitch. Multiple polls demonstrate that most Americans aren’t buying Trump’s $5,000 dividend promises or don’t think it’s a good idea. An NBC News poll published on Sunday showed that nearly half of self-identified Republicans don’t expect the payment.
 More articles
 The interests of Americans take a back seat to Trump’s kingly demands 
 Chris Hayes 
 A new poll shows a record number of Americans worry about Trump’s economy 
 James Downie 
 What if the cash at stake wasn’t $90 but $2,000? That was the case for Tim Lilienthal, a Utah-based independent consultant and leadership coach. Earlier this month, he received a letter that touted Trump’s healthcare record, along with a paper check bearing the hefty sum.
 “My wife and I were so disgusted by it, we didn’t cash it for a week,” Lilienthal said. “We just let it sit on our dining room table. Because I just was like, I don’t even want it. It felt like a bribe.”
 For now, Republicans are saying little about the Medicare and Obamacare checks and focusing on limiting their probable losses in the midterms.
 Lilienthal, a Republican who didn’t vote for Trump in the last election, lost his ACA subsidies when the GOP-held Congress failed to extend them. When all was said and done, his household’s monthly bill shot up from $1,475 to $2,623 — a 78% increase in premium costs for a family of four. Lilienthal’s 11-year old son helped him overcome the anguish about the check and put the $2,000 into 529 college savings plans.
 Whether the president knows it or not, Trump is copying the playbook of populist governments with awful economic track records. It’s a simple tactic: Pull out all the stops to win votes now and worry about the cost later.
 In 2018, ex-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro dangled a reward for Venezuelans if they supported him in what was a presidential election later marred by fraud.
 “You give, I give. I am thinking of giving a prize to the people of Venezuela who come out and vote,” he said at the time , linking a government handout in exchange for their vote.
 In Argentina, politicians have used election-related giveaways to cobble together constituencies for decades. In Sept. 2023, then-Economic Minister Sergio Massa campaigned for the presidency and announced a financial relief package timed just before the election. The plan platita — or “pocket cash plan” — delivered a mix of subsidies , tax exemptions and $256 cash handouts to retirees, public-sector employees, self-employed workers and even professionals. Voters, though, ultimately handed control of Argentina’s government to Javier Milei, a slash-and-burn libertarian who pledged to tackle inflation no matter what.
 American voters may well be inclined to reject the last-ditch handouts, too.
 “As a voter, it shows desperation to me,” Butler said, calling the cash payment “dirty money” that she wanted nothing to do with. For now, Republicans are saying little about the Medicare and Obamacare checks and focusing on limiting their probable losses in the midterms.
 “I hadn’t heard much on this from constituents,” Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, an occasional Trump critic who’s floating a 2028 presidential run, said in a text message.
 “I’ve been more focused on the $5K promises and what’s going on in Ukraine at the moment,” Bacon said.
 It’s hard to turn down free money, especially when prices keep scaling to new heights with little end in sight. In this case, it amounts to pocket change that falls far short in assembling a political coalition that will stem the bleeding for Republicans in the midterms — and they’re on the cusp of paying the price.
 Joseph Zeballos-Roig 
 Joseph Zeballos-Roig is a reporter who has covered economic policy and politics for Semafor, Business Insider and Quartz, among other publications.
